"""
Antioch Demo Splash Screen

This splash screen displays while Pyodide loads, providing SEO-friendly
static HTML content for search engines and a better user experience.
"""

from antioch.static import StaticPage, Div, P, keyframe, rotate, opacity, translateY

# Sky-strata-sky: blue fading to the icon's own sky color, a thin band of the
# strata browns across the middle, then back out to blue.
DEEP_BLUE = "#305a88"
SKY_BLUE = "#99b1cb"  # sampled from assets/sed_stats.png
STRATA = ["#ccc3ba", "#b2a48a", "#9c8969", "#9e6549", "#8e5b42", "#665141"]

BAND_START, BAND_END = 35, 65

# The sky reaches full light blue this far short of the band, leaving a stretch
# for it to wash into the first brown instead of meeting it at a hard edge.
BLEND = 5


def strata_gradient(angle="135deg"):
    """The background gradient, with the browns held to the middle band."""
    span = BAND_END - BAND_START
    stops = [f"{DEEP_BLUE} 0%", f"{SKY_BLUE} {BAND_START - BLEND}%"]
    for i, color in enumerate(STRATA):
        position = BAND_START + span * i / (len(STRATA) - 1)
        stops.append(f"{color} {position:g}%")
    stops.append(f"{SKY_BLUE} {BAND_END + BLEND}%")
    stops.append(f"{DEEP_BLUE} 100%")
    return f"linear-gradient({angle}, {', '.join(stops)})"


# Define keyframe animations pythonically!
@keyframe
def spin():
    rotate({0: 0, 100: 360})


@keyframe
def fadeInDown():
    opacity({0: 0, 100: 1})
    translateY({0: -30, 100: 0})


@keyframe
def fadeInUp():
    opacity({0: 0, 100: 1})
    translateY({0: 30, 100: 0})


def generate_splash():
    """Generate the static splash screen HTML."""

    # Create the page with SEO metadata
    page = StaticPage(title="Sed/Stats", lang="en")
    page.set_title("Sed/Stats")
    page.add_meta(
        name="viewport",
        content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0, maximum-scale=1.0, user-scalable=no"
    )

    # SEO Meta Tags
    page.set_description(
        "Sed/Stats is a web app that facilitates visualization and interpretation of sedimentological data"
        "Upload your data and generate high-quality, publication-ready figures in just a few clicks."
    )
    page.set_keywords("sedimentology", "geology", "detrital zircon", "python", "mixture modeling", "microplastics")
    page.set_author("Ryan Nielsen")

    # Open Graph tags for social media
    page.set_og_title("Sed/Stats")
    page.set_og_description("Build publication-ready figures in just a few clicks")
    page.set_og_url("https://sedstats.com")

    # Add animations to page
    page.add_style(spin.render())
    page.add_style(fadeInDown.render())
    page.add_style(fadeInUp.render())

    # Set body styles using dictionary assignment (just like DOM.body.style in Antioch!)
    page_div = Div(style = {
        'margin': '0',
        'padding': '0',
        'font_family': '-apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, "Segoe UI", Roboto, "Helvetica Neue", Arial, sans-serif',
        'background': strata_gradient(),
        'min_height': '100vh',
        'display': 'flex',
        'justify_content': 'center',
        'align_items': 'center',
        'color': 'white'
    })


    # Build the splash screen content with pythonic styles
    container = Div(id="loading-splash", style={
        'text-align': 'center',
        'padding': '40px',
        'max-width': '600px'
    })

    # Logo with gradient text effect
    logo = Div("Sed/Stats", style={
        'font-size': '4em',
        'font-weight': 'bold',
        'margin-bottom': '20px',
        'background': 'linear-gradient(135deg, #fff 0%, #f0f0f0 100%)',
        '-webkit-background-clip': 'text',
        '-webkit-text-fill-color': 'transparent',
        'background-clip': 'text'
    })

    # Tagline
    tagline = P("Visualize and Interpret Sedimentological Data", style={
        'font-size': '1.5em',
        'margin-bottom': '30px',
        'opacity': '0.9',
        'animation': 'fadeInUp 0.8s ease-out 0.2s both'
    })

    # Spinner
    spinner_container = Div(style={
        'margin': '30px auto 20px auto',
        'animation': 'fadeInUp 0.8s ease-out 0.6s both'
    })
    spinner = Div(style={
        'border': '4px solid rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.3)',
        'border-top': '4px solid white',
        'border-radius': '50%',
        'width': '60px',
        'height': '60px',
        'animation': 'spin 1s linear infinite',
        'margin': '0 auto'
    })
    spinner_container.add(spinner)

    # Loading text
    loading_text = P("Loading modules...", style={
        'font-size': '1.1em',
        'margin': '0',
        'opacity': '0.8'
    })

    # Add all elements to container
    container.add(logo, tagline, spinner_container, loading_text)
    page_div.add(container)
    page.add(page_div)

    return page


# Allow running this file directly to preview the splash screen
if __name__ == "__main__":
    import sys
    from pathlib import Path

    # Add parent directory to path to import antioch.static
    sys.path.insert(0, str(Path(__file__).parent.parent))

    page = generate_splash()
    preview_path = Path(__file__).parent.parent / "splash_preview.html"

    with open(preview_path, "w") as f:
        f.write(page.render())

    print(f"✅ Splash screen preview saved to: {preview_path}")
    print(f"   Open it in a browser to see how it looks!")

"""
Sed/Stats

Editor-style layout: an Outputs tab holding a tool menu and the generated
graphs, and a Spreadsheet tab holding the data. Tools are grouped into
Univariate and Multivariate menus; each opens a wizard that collects samples,
dimensions and options, and graphs are produced
only on demand. Selecting several dimensions yields one tabbed output with a
tab per dimension. Data comes from the built-in example, an uploaded
csv/xls/xlsx file, or a file opened from the user's Google Drive.

The pieces live in the `dashboard` package; this module only assembles them.
"""
import asyncio

from antioch.event import when
from antioch import DOM
from dashboard import AppShell, build_tools
from ui_lib import LoadingOverlay


def main():
    DOM.clear()
    DOM.title = "Sed/Stats"
    shell = AppShell()
    overlay = LoadingOverlay()

    tools = build_tools(
        get_rows=shell.table.get_data,
        gallery=shell.gallery,
        overlay=overlay,
        # The PCA axes tool writes derived columns back; set_data fires
        # data_change, which re-syncs every tool's dimension list.
        set_rows=shell.table.set_data,
    )

    # The toolbar opens tools, so it can only be wired once they exist.
    shell.set_tool_menu(tools)

    def sync_tool_options(*args, **kwargs):
        rows = shell.table.get_data()
        for tool in tools.values():
            tool.sync_options(rows)

    sync_tool_options()

    # If the user connected Google before, re-attach silently. Google
    # re-issues a token with no UI while the grant is live, so a reload keeps
    # them signed in; if it cannot, they just see the sign-in button again.
    asyncio.ensure_future(shell.drive.restore())

    @when(shell.tabs.events.change)
    def on_top_tab(sender, tab, *args):
        # Both widgets measure themselves on render and read zero while hidden.
        if tab.title == "Spreadsheet":
            shell.table.redraw()
        else:
            shell.gallery.resize_all()

    @when(shell.table.events.data_change)
    def on_table_change(sender, *args):
        sync_tool_options()

    def load_rows(rows):
        """Put a freshly parsed spreadsheet into the grid."""
        try:
            shell.table.set_data(rows)
            sync_tool_options()
        finally:
            # Whatever happens, the curtain has to come back up.
            overlay.hide()

    # Parsing a large workbook and handing it to Tabulator both block the UI
    # thread, so loading a file gets the same overlay as generating a graph.
    # Both loaders announce load_start, and both always finish with
    # data_loaded or error.
    for loader in (shell.upload, shell.drive):
        @when(loader.events.load_start)
        def on_load_start(sender, filename, *args):
            overlay.show(f"Loading {filename}…")

        @when(loader.events.data_loaded)
        def on_loaded(sender, rows, filename, *args):
            load_rows(rows)

        @when(loader.events.error)
        def on_load_error(sender, message, *args):
            overlay.hide()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

"""Packaging plots for download."""
import io
import re
import zipfile

import js
from pyodide.ffi import to_js


def safe_filename(name, fallback="chart"):
    cleaned = re.sub(r"[^A-Za-z0-9._-]+", "_", str(name)).strip("_")
    return cleaned or fallback


async def charts_to_zip(named_charts):
    """
    Zip several plots' SVGs into one archive.

    Args:
        named_charts: [(name, PlotlyChart), ...]

    Returns:
        bytes of the .zip
    """
    buffer = io.BytesIO()
    used = set()
    with zipfile.ZipFile(buffer, "w", zipfile.ZIP_DEFLATED) as archive:
        for name, chart in named_charts:
            base = safe_filename(name)
            filename = base
            index = 2
            while filename in used:
                filename = f"{base}_{index}"
                index += 1
            used.add(filename)
            archive.writestr(f"{filename}.svg", await chart.to_svg())
    return buffer.getvalue()


def download_bytes(data, filename, mime="application/zip"):
    """Hand a bytes payload to the browser as a download."""
    array = js.Uint8Array.new(len(data))
    array.assign(data)
    blob = js.Blob.new(
        [array], to_js({"type": mime}, dict_converter=js.Object.fromEntries)
    )
    url = js.URL.createObjectURL(blob)

    anchor = js.document.createElement("a")
    anchor.href = url
    anchor.download = filename
    js.document.body.appendChild(anchor)
    anchor.click()
    js.document.body.removeChild(anchor)
    js.URL.revokeObjectURL(url)

"""Plotly-backed chart macro.

Plotly renders cartesian plots as real SVG in the DOM, so vector export is
native rather than a rasterized canvas snapshot.

Uses the `cartesian` bundle rather than `basic`: basic registers only bar, pie
and scatter, and the bivariate density plots need heatmap.
"""
import js

from antioch.elements import Div
from antioch.macros.js_library import JSLibraryMacro


class PlotlyChart(JSLibraryMacro):
    """
    Chart backed by plotly.js.

    Usage:
        chart = PlotlyChart(
            traces=[{"type": "bar", "x": ["a", "b"], "y": [1, 2], "name": "S1"}],
            layout={"title": {"text": "Counts"}},
        )
        DOM.add(chart.element)
        chart.download_svg("counts")
    """

    def __init__(self, traces=None, layout=None, config=None,
                 width=760, height=420, **kwargs):
        """
        Args:
            traces: List of plotly trace dicts
            layout: Plotly layout dict, merged over the defaults
            config: Plotly config dict, merged over the defaults
            width/height: Plot size in pixels
        """
        super().__init__(macro_type="plotly_chart", **kwargs)

        self._set_state(
            traces=traces or [],
            layout=layout or {},
            config=config or {},
            width=width,
            height=height,
        )

        self._init_macro()

    def _get_library_dependencies(self):
        return {
            'scripts': ['antioch/lib/vendor/plotly-cartesian.min.js'],
            'stylesheets': [],
        }

    def _get_library_global_name(self):
        return 'Plotly'

    def _create_elements(self):
        container = self._register_element(
            'container', self._create_container({"width": "100%"})
        )
        holder = self._register_element('holder', Div())
        holder.set_attribute("id", f"plotly_{self._id}")
        container.add(holder)
        return container

    def _build_layout(self):
        layout = {
            'width': self._get_state('width'),
            'height': self._get_state('height'),
            'margin': {'l': 60, 'r': 20, 't': 50, 'b': 50},
            'font': {'size': 12},
            'hovermode': 'closest',
            'showlegend': True,
        }
        layout.update(self._get_state('layout'))
        return layout

    def _build_config(self):
        config = {
            'displaylogo': False,
            'displayModeBar': True,  # always visible; hover-to-reveal is unusable on touch
            'responsive': False,
            # Makes the modebar's camera button emit SVG instead of PNG.
            'toImageButtonOptions': {'format': 'svg', 'filename': 'chart'},
        }
        config.update(self._get_state('config'))
        return config

    def _create_js_instance(self):
        # Plotly's API is keyed on the graph div itself, so that element is the
        # instance. newPlot returns a promise we don't need to await: every
        # later call goes through the same div.
        graph_div = self._get_element('holder')._dom_element
        js.Plotly.newPlot(
            graph_div,
            self._to_js(self._get_state('traces')),
            self._to_js(self._build_layout()),
            self._to_js(self._build_config()),
        )
        return graph_div

    def _cleanup_js_instance(self):
        if self.js_instance:
            js.Plotly.purge(self.js_instance)

    # ========== Public API ==========

    def update(self, traces=None, layout=None):
        """Re-render with new traces/layout via Plotly.react (diffed, not rebuilt)."""
        self.ensure_initialized()
        if traces is not None:
            self._set_state(traces=traces)
        if layout is not None:
            self._set_state(layout=layout)
        js.Plotly.react(
            self.js_instance,
            self._to_js(self._get_state('traces')),
            self._to_js(self._build_layout()),
            self._to_js(self._build_config()),
        )
        return self

    async def to_svg(self):
        """The plot's SVG markup, for callers that want to package it up."""
        self.ensure_initialized()
        data_uri = await js.Plotly.toImage(self.js_instance, self._to_js({
            'format': 'svg',
            'width': self._get_state('width'),
            'height': self._get_state('height'),
        }))
        # Plotly returns "data:image/svg+xml,<percent-encoded markup>"
        return js.decodeURIComponent(data_uri.split(",", 1)[1])

    def download_svg(self, filename="chart"):
        """Trigger a browser download of the plot as SVG."""
        self.ensure_initialized()
        js.Plotly.downloadImage(self.js_instance, self._to_js({
            'format': 'svg',
            'filename': filename,
            'width': self._get_state('width'),
            'height': self._get_state('height'),
        }))
        return self

    def resize(self):
        """Re-fit the plot to its container, after becoming visible again."""
        if self.is_initialized:
            js.Plotly.Plots.resize(self.js_instance)
        return self

    @property
    def is_ready(self):
        return self.is_initialized

"""Builders for the plotly trace dicts this project uses.""" def subplot_axes(row: int): """Axis names for a trace in a given 0-indexed subplot row.""" suffix = "" if row == 0 else str(row + 1) return f"x{suffix}", f"y{suffix}" def stacked_subplot_layout(rows: int, vertical_spacing=None, shared_xaxis=False): """ Axis layout for `rows` subplots stacked top to bottom. plotly.js has no make_subplots helper — subplots are just multiple axes with stacked `domain` ranges — so this reproduces what `make_subplots(rows=n, cols=1)` generates, including its default spacing of 0.3/rows and its top-to-bottom row ordering. """ if rows < 1: return {} if vertical_spacing is None: vertical_spacing = 0.3 / rows if rows > 1 else 0.0 height = (1.0 - vertical_spacing * (rows - 1)) / rows layout = {} for row in range(rows): x_name, y_name = subplot_axes(row) suffix = "" if row == 0 else str(row + 1) top = 1.0 - row * (height + vertical_spacing) bottom = max(0.0, top - height) layout[f"xaxis{suffix}"] = { "anchor": y_name, "domain": [0.0, 1.0], # Only the bottom row keeps tick labels when axes are shared "showticklabels": True if not shared_xaxis else (row == rows - 1), } layout[f"yaxis{suffix}"] = { "anchor": x_name, "domain": [round(bottom, 4), round(top, 4)], } return layout def subplot_title(row: int, text: str): """Annotation that labels one subplot, as make_subplots' subplot_titles do.""" _, y_name = subplot_axes(row) return { "text": text, "showarrow": False, "xref": "paper", "yref": f"{y_name} domain", "x": 0.0, "y": 1.0, "xanchor": "left", "yanchor": "bottom", "font": {"size": 12}, } # White at zero so empty grid reads as blank page rather than "cold", which is # how Sundell & Saylor (2021) present bivariate density. DENSITY_COLORSCALE = [ [0.0, "#ffffff"], [0.05, "#e8eef7"], [0.25, "#3b6fb6"], [0.5, "#2ec4b6"], [0.75, "#f5c542"], [1.0, "#c1121f"], ] def heatmap_trace(x, y, z, name=None, colorscale=None, colorbar_title=None, show_scale=True): """ A density grid. `z` is row-major with one row per y value. Args: x, y: axis coordinates z: nested sequence, len(y) rows of len(x) colorbar_title: label beside the scale bar """ # Coerced to plain floats: these axes usually arrive as numpy arrays, and # numpy scalars do not cross the Pyodide boundary cleanly. trace = { "type": "heatmap", "x": [float(v) for v in x], "y": [float(v) for v in y], "z": [[float(v) for v in row] for row in z], "colorscale": colorscale or DENSITY_COLORSCALE, "showscale": show_scale, "zsmooth": "best", } if name: trace["name"] = name if colorbar_title: trace["colorbar"] = {"title": {"text": colorbar_title, "side": "right"}} return trace def series_color(index: int, total: int) -> str: """Evenly spaced hues, so series stay distinguishable at any count.""" return f"hsl({round(360 * index / max(total, 1))}, 70%, 45%)" def bar_trace(x, y, name, color=None): trace = {"type": "bar", "x": list(x), "y": list(y), "name": name} if color: trace["marker"] = {"color": color} return trace def line_trace(x, y, name, color=None, markers=False): """A line. Markers are off by default — on a kernel curve with hundreds of grid points they turn the line into a solid smear.""" trace = { "type": "scatter", "mode": "lines+markers" if markers else "lines", "x": list(x), "y": list(y), "name": name, } if color: trace["line"] = {"color": color, "width": 2} trace["marker"] = {"color": color, "size": 5} return trace def error_bar_trace(x, y, errors, name, color=None, size=9): """Points with symmetric vertical error bars.""" trace = { "type": "scatter", "mode": "markers", "x": list(x), "y": list(y), "name": name, "error_y": { "type": "data", "array": [float(e) for e in errors], "visible": True, "thickness": 1.5, "width": 6, }, } if color: trace["marker"] = {"color": color, "size": size} trace["error_y"]["color"] = color else: trace["marker"] = {"size": size} return trace def marker_trace(x, y, name, color=None, labels=None, size=10): """Scatter points, optionally annotated with per-point text labels.""" trace = { "type": "scatter", "mode": "markers+text" if labels else "markers", "x": list(x), "y": list(y), "name": name, } if labels: trace["text"] = list(labels) trace["textposition"] = "top center" trace["textfont"] = {"size": 10} if color: trace["marker"] = {"color": color, "size": size} else: trace["marker"] = {"size": size} return trace # Fixed categorical palette, in fixed order — never generated, never cycled by # rank. Validated for adjacent pairs in both modes; see SCATTER_CAP below for # the tighter limit that applies to scatter plots. CATEGORICAL_PALETTE = [ "#2a78d6", # blue "#eb6834", # orange "#1baf7a", # aqua "#eda100", # yellow "#e87ba4", # magenta "#008300", # green "#4a3aa7", # violet "#e34948", # red ] # On a scatter every series can touch every other, so all pairs must separate, # not just adjacent ones. " f"{hover_y}: %{{y}}"), } if color: trace["marker"]["color"] = color return trace def ternary_trace(a, b, c, name, color=None, symbol=None, size=7, opacity=0.8, labels=None, apex_names=("a", "b", "c")): """ Points on a ternary diagram. " f"{apex_names[0]}: %{{a:.1f}}
" f"{apex_names[1]}: %{{b:.1f}}
" f"{apex_names[2]}: %{{c:.1f}}" ), } if color: trace["marker"]["color"] = color if labels: trace["mode"] = "markers+text" trace["text"] = list(labels) trace["textposition"] = "top center" trace["textfont"] = {"size": 10} return trace def ternary_layout(apex_names, total=100, show_ticks=True): """ Layout overrides that turn a figure into a ternary one. """
Principal component analysis over per-sample distributions.

Each sample is one observation and every grid position is a feature, so a set
of distributions becomes an (n_samples, n_points) matrix. The first two
components are the plane that captures the most variance between samples.

This is the linear counterpart to sed_stats.mds: MDS starts from a pairwise
dissimilarity matrix and only preserves rank order or distance, whereas PCA
works on the distributions themselves and so can also report *which* parts of
the distribution drive the separation, via the component loadings.

Computation only — plotting is left to the caller.
"""
import numpy as np


class PCAPoint:
    """One sample's position in component space."""

    def __init__(self, x: float, y: float, label: str):
        self.x = x
        self.y = y
        self.label = label

    def __repr__(self):
        return f"PCAPoint({self.label!r}, {self.x:.4g}, {self.y:.4g})"


class PCAResult:
    """
    Attributes:
        points          - PCAPoint per sample, in the order given
        scores          - (n_samples, n_components) coordinates
        components      - (n_components, n_features) loadings, one row per PC
        explained_ratio - fraction of total variance per component
        mean            - the feature mean that was subtracted
        singular_values - from the SVD, for a scree plot
    """

    def __init__(self, points, scores, components, explained_ratio, mean,
                 singular_values, explained_ratio_all=None, blocks=None):
        self.points = points
        self.scores = scores
        self.components = components
        self.explained_ratio = explained_ratio
        self.mean = mean
        self.singular_values = singular_values
        # Every component, not just the kept ones — a scree plot needs the tail
        # to show where the useful variance stops.
        self.explained_ratio_all = (explained_ratio if explained_ratio_all is None
                                    else explained_ratio_all)
        # [(variable_name, start, stop), ...] when the feature vector was
        # concatenated from several variables; empty for a single-variable PCA.
        self.blocks = blocks or []

    def percent(self, component: int) -> float:
        """Percent of variance explained by a 0-indexed component."""
        if component >= self.explained_ratio.size:
            return 0.0
        return float(self.explained_ratio[component] * 100)

    def block_contributions(self, component: int):
        """
        How much each variable drives a component, as fractions summing to 1.

        Only meaningful for a combined_pca result. Component rows are unit
        vectors, so the squared loadings inside one variable's slice are that
        variable's share of the component.

        Returns:
            [(name, fraction), ...], or [] when the PCA was over one variable
        """
        if not self.blocks or component >= self.components.shape[0]:
            return []
        loadings = self.components[component] ** 2
        total = float(loadings.sum()) or 1.0
        return [(name, float(loadings[start:stop].sum()) / total)
                for name, start, stop in self.blocks]


class GrainPCAResult:
    """
    A PCA fitted across individual measurements rather than whole samples.

    Attributes:
        scores          - (n_grains, n_components) per-grain coordinates
        components      - (n_components, n_variables) loadings
        explained_ratio - fraction of total variance per component
        variables       - the variable names, in column order
        mean, scale     - the standardization that was applied
    """

    def __init__(self, scores, components, explained_ratio, variables,
                 mean, scale, explained_ratio_all=None):
        self.scores = scores
        self.components = components
        self.explained_ratio = explained_ratio
        self.variables = list(variables)
        self.mean = mean
        self.scale = scale
        self.explained_ratio_all = (explained_ratio if explained_ratio_all is None
                                    else explained_ratio_all)

    def percent(self, component: int) -> float:
        if component >= self.explained_ratio.size:
            return 0.0
        return float(self.explained_ratio[component] * 100)

    def loadings(self, component: int):
        """[(variable, loading), ...] for one component, largest first."""
        if component >= self.components.shape[0]:
            return []
        pairs = list(zip(self.variables, self.components[component]))
        return sorted(pairs, key=lambda pair: abs(pair[1]), reverse=True)


def grain_pca(matrix, variables=None, n_components: int = 2,
              weights=None) -> GrainPCAResult:
    """
    Fit one PCA across every measurement, for use as a derived axis.

    This is the transform that makes multivariate top-down unmixing work. A
    mixture of grain populations produces a distribution that is a convex
    combination of its sources' distributions, and that stays true under any
    fixed per-grain map — so projecting every grain onto a single, globally
    fitted PC1 gives a new scalar whose distributions still mix linearly.

    Two things it therefore must NOT do, both of which would break that
    property: fit separately per sample, or standardize per sample. The fit and
    the standardization are global, over the pooled measurements.

    Args:
        matrix: (n_grains, n_variables), every grain from every sample
        variables: column names, for reporting the loadings
        n_components: how many components to keep
        weights: optional per-grain weight. Pass 1/n for each grain of a
            sample to stop a sample with many analyses from dominating the
            axis; the projection itself stays unweighted.

    Raises:
        ValueError: with fewer than two grains or fewer than two variables
    """
    matrix = np.asarray(matrix, dtype=float)
    if matrix.ndim != 2:
        raise ValueError("Expected a (grains, variables) matrix")
    n_grains, n_variables = matrix.shape
    if n_grains < 2:
        raise ValueError("Need at least two measurements")
    if n_variables < 2:
        raise ValueError("Need at least two variables")

    if variables is None:
        variables = [f"v{i + 1}" for i in range(n_variables)]

    if weights is None:
        weight_vector = np.ones(n_grains)
    else:
        weight_vector = np.asarray(weights, dtype=float)
        if weight_vector.shape[0] != n_grains:
            raise ValueError("weights must be one per measurement")
    total_weight = float(weight_vector.sum()) or 1.0

    mean = (weight_vector @ matrix) / total_weight
    centered = matrix - mean

    # Standardize: variables in different units (Ma, °C, ratios) would
    # otherwise be ranked by the size of their numbers, not their information.
    variance = (weight_vector @ (centered ** 2)) / total_weight
    scale = np.sqrt(variance)
    scale[scale <= 0] = 1.0  # a constant column carries nothing either way
    standardized = centered / scale

    # The SVD is weighted; the projection is not, so every grain still lands at
    # its own honest position on the axis.
    weighted = standardized * np.sqrt(weight_vector)[:, np.newaxis]
    _, singular_values, right = np.linalg.svd(weighted, full_matrices=False)

    n_components = max(1, min(n_components, n_variables))
    components = right[:n_components].copy()
    scores = standardized @ components.T
    components, scores = _flip_signs(components, scores)

    total = float(np.sum(singular_values ** 2))
    explained_ratio = (singular_values ** 2 / total) if total > 0 else \
        np.zeros_like(singular_values)

    return GrainPCAResult(
        scores=scores,
        components=components,
        explained_ratio=explained_ratio[:n_components],
        explained_ratio_all=explained_ratio,
        variables=variables,
        mean=mean,
        scale=scale,
    )


def _flip_signs(components, scores):
    """
    Pin the arbitrary sign of each component.

    An SVD is only defined up to a sign per component, so an unpinned plot can
    come out mirrored for no reason. Forcing the largest-magnitude loading
    positive makes the orientation reproducible.
    """
    for i in range(components.shape[0]):
        largest = int(np.argmax(np.abs(components[i])))
        if components[i, largest] < 0:
            components[i] *= -1
            scores[:, i] *= -1
    return components, scores


def _decompose(centered, sample_names, mean, n_components, blocks=None) -> PCAResult:
    """The shared SVD core, on an already-centered matrix."""
    n_samples, n_features = centered.shape
    # An n-sample set spans at most n-1 dimensions once it is centered.
    n_components = max(1, min(n_components, n_samples - 1, n_features))

    # SVD rather than an eigendecomposition of the covariance matrix: there are
    # far more grid points than samples, so the covariance matrix would be huge
    # and rank-deficient.
    _, singular_values, right = np.linalg.svd(centered, full_matrices=False)

    components = right[:n_components].copy()
    scores = centered @ components.T
    components, scores = _flip_signs(components, scores)

    total = float(np.sum(singular_values ** 2))
    explained_ratio = (singular_values ** 2 / total) if total > 0 else \
        np.zeros_like(singular_values)

    points = [
        PCAPoint(float(scores[i, 0]),
                 float(scores[i, 1]) if n_components > 1 else 0.0,
                 name)
        for i, name in enumerate(sample_names)
    ]

    return PCAResult(
        points=points,
        scores=scores,
        components=components,
        explained_ratio=explained_ratio[:n_components],
        explained_ratio_all=explained_ratio,
        mean=mean,
        singular_values=singular_values,
        blocks=blocks,
    )


def pca_function(series, n_components: int = 2) -> PCAResult:
    """
    Run PCA on a list of (sample_name, values) pairs.

    Args:
        series: every sample's distribution, all on the same grid
        n_components: how many components to keep

    Returns:
        PCAResult

    Raises:
        ValueError: with fewer than two samples, or ragged distributions
    """
    if len(series) < 2:
        raise ValueError("PCA needs at least two samples")

    matrix = np.asarray([np.asarray(values, dtype=float) for _, values in series])
    if matrix.ndim != 2:
        raise ValueError("Every sample must be on the same grid")

    mean = matrix.mean(axis=0)
    return _decompose(matrix - mean, [name for name, _ in series], mean,
                      n_components)


def combined_pca(blocks, sample_names, n_components: int = 2,
                 weighting: str = "equal") -> PCAResult:
    """
    One PCA over several variables at once.

    Each sample's feature vector is its distribution for every variable laid
    end to end, so the result answers "how do these samples relate given
    everything measured" rather than one variable at a time.

    Args:
        blocks: [(variable_name, matrix)], each matrix (n_samples, n_features_i)
                with rows in the same sample order
        sample_names: one per row, shared by every block
        n_components: how many components to keep
        weighting: "equal" divides each variable by its own first singular
                   value, so a variable cannot dominate merely by having a
                   longer grid or larger numbers (Escofier & Pages' multiple
                   factor analysis). "none" concatenates raw.

    Raises:
        ValueError: with no blocks, fewer than two samples, or mismatched rows
    """
    if not blocks:
        raise ValueError("Need at least one variable")
    if len(sample_names) < 2:
        raise ValueError("PCA needs at least two samples")

    pieces = []
    spans = []
    start = 0
    for name, matrix in blocks:
        matrix = np.asarray(matrix, dtype=float)
        if matrix.shape[0] != len(sample_names):
            raise ValueError(f"'{name}' has {matrix.shape[0]} rows, "
                             f"expected {len(sample_names)}")
        centered = matrix - matrix.mean(axis=0)

        scale = 1.0
        if weighting == "equal":
            values = np.linalg.svd(centered, compute_uv=False)
            if values.size and values[0] > 0:
                scale = float(values[0])

        pieces.append(centered / scale)
        spans.append((name, start, start + centered.shape[1]))
        start += centered.shape[1]

    # Every block was centered on its own, so the concatenation already is.
    combined = np.hstack(pieces)
    return _decompose(combined, list(sample_names),
                      np.zeros(combined.shape[1]), n_components, blocks=spans)

"""
Multidimensional scaling by majorization, and the isotonic fit it needs.

These replace scikit-learn's `manifold.MDS` and `isotonic.IsotonicRegression`.
Not for want of trust in those — they are the reference this was checked
against — but for weight: scikit-learn drags SciPy behind it, and the pair
costs about 19 MB of the roughly 22 MB this app downloads before it can run.
Two algorithms of a hundred lines each is a fair trade for that.

SMACOF (Scaling by MAjorizing A COmplicated Function, de Leeuw 1977) minimises
Kruskal's raw stress

    sigma(X) = sum over i<j of (d_ij(X) - dhat_ij)^2

by repeatedly applying the Guttman transform, which is guaranteed not to
increase the stress. In metric MDS the target dhat is the dissimilarity
itself; in non-metric MDS it is whatever monotonically increasing function of
the dissimilarities best fits the current distances — which is what the
isotonic regression supplies.
"""
import numpy as np


def isotonic_regression(x, y, weights=None) -> np.ndarray:
    """
    Fit a non-decreasing step function of `x` to `y`, by least squares.

    Pool Adjacent Violators: walk the points in order of `x` keeping a stack
    of blocks, and whenever a new block's mean falls below its predecessor's
    merge the two. Merging can cascade, but each point joins and leaves a
    block at most once, so the whole pass is linear.

    Ties in `x` are averaged before fitting. Without that, two points sharing
    an x could be given different fitted values, and the result would not be a
    function of x at all.

    Returns:
        Fitted values, in the order the inputs were given.
    """
    x = np.asarray(x, dtype=float)
    y = np.asarray(y, dtype=float)
    if x.shape != y.shape:
        raise ValueError("x and y must be the same length")
    if x.size == 0:
        return np.array([], dtype=float)

    w = np.ones(x.size) if weights is None else np.asarray(weights, dtype=float)

    # Stable sort, so equal x keep their input order and group together.
    order = np.argsort(x, kind="mergesort")
    x_sorted, y_sorted, w_sorted = x[order], y[order], w[order]

    # Collapse ties into one weighted point each. reduceat rather than a
    # comprehension over np.split: non-metric SMACOF calls this once per
    # iteration per restart, so it is genuinely hot.
    starts = np.concatenate(([0], np.flatnonzero(np.diff(x_sorted)) + 1))
    sizes = np.diff(np.append(starts, x_sorted.size))
    group_weight = np.add.reduceat(w_sorted, starts)
    weighted = np.add.reduceat(w_sorted * y_sorted, starts)
    group_value = np.where(group_weight > 0,
                           weighted / np.where(group_weight > 0, group_weight, 1),
                           np.add.reduceat(y_sorted, starts) / sizes)

    # PAVA over the collapsed points.
    value = np.empty(group_value.size)
    weight = np.empty(group_value.size)
    count = np.empty(group_value.size, dtype=int)
    top = 0
    for index in range(group_value.size):
        value[top] = group_value[index]
        weight[top] = group_weight[index]
        count[top] = 1
        while top > 0 and value[top - 1] > value[top]:
            combined = weight[top - 1] + weight[top]
            value[top - 1] = (
                (weight[top - 1] * value[top - 1] + weight[top] * value[top])
                / combined if combined > 0
                else (value[top - 1] + value[top]) / 2
            )
            weight[top - 1] = combined
            count[top - 1] += count[top]
            top -= 1
        top += 1

    # Back out to every original point: block value -> group -> input order.
    per_group = np.repeat(value[:top], count[:top])
    fitted = np.empty(x.size)
    fitted[order] = np.repeat(per_group, sizes)
    return fitted


def _pairwise_distances(points: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    """Euclidean distance matrix, with an exact zero diagonal."""
    squared = np.sum(points ** 2, axis=1)
    gram = points @ points.T
    distances = squared[:, None] + squared[None, :] - 2 * gram
    np.maximum(distances, 0, out=distances)
    np.sqrt(distances, out=distances)
    np.fill_diagonal(distances, 0.0)
    return distances


def classical_mds(dissimilarities: np.ndarray, n_components: int = 2) -> np.ndarray:
    """
    Torgerson scaling: an eigen-decomposition that lands near the answer.

    Used as SMACOF's starting point. A random start needs many restarts to
    avoid a poor local minimum; starting from the classical solution usually
    converges to a better one, and does so in the same place every time.
    """
    n = dissimilarities.shape[0]
    squared = dissimilarities ** 2
    # Double centering turns squared distances into a Gram matrix.
    centering = np.eye(n) - np.ones((n, n)) / n
    gram = -0.5 * centering @ squared @ centering
    gram = (gram + gram.T) / 2  # symmetrize away the rounding

    values, vectors = np.linalg.eigh(gram)
    # eigh returns ascending; the largest eigenvalues carry the structure.
    order = np.argsort(values)[::-1][:n_components]
    values, vectors = values[order], vectors[:, order]
    return vectors * np.sqrt(np.maximum(values, 0))


def _stress_1(distances, fitted) -> float:
    """
    Kruskal's stress-1: the residual, normalised by the distances themselves.

    Scale-invariant, which raw stress is not — and in non-metric MDS the
    configuration's overall size is free, so raw stress cannot be compared
    between runs at all. A configuration collapsing toward a point would post
    a flatteringly small raw stress while fitting nothing.
    """
    total = float(np.sum(distances ** 2))
    if total <= 0:
        return 1.0  # everything on top of everything: the worst possible fit
    return float(np.sqrt(np.sum((distances - fitted) ** 2) / total))


def _smacof_single(dissimilarities, n_components, metric, max_iter, eps,
                   init=None, rng=None):
    """One SMACOF run. Returns (embedding, stress-1, iterations)."""
    n = dissimilarities.shape[0]
    upper = np.triu_indices(n, k=1)
    delta = dissimilarities[upper]

    if init is not None:
        points = np.array(init, dtype=float)
    else:
        points = rng.uniform(-1.0, 1.0, size=(n, n_components))

    target = np.empty((n, n))
    previous = None
    stress = 0.0
    iteration = 0

    for iteration in range(1, max_iter + 1):
        distance_matrix = _pairwise_distances(points)
        distances = distance_matrix[upper]

        if metric:
            fitted = delta
        else:
            # The monotone transform of the dissimilarities that best matches
            # the current distances, rescaled to fix the arbitrary overall
            # size that a rank-only target would otherwise leave free.
            fitted = isotonic_regression(delta, distances)
            norm = np.sqrt(np.sum(fitted ** 2))
            if norm > 0:
                fitted = fitted * np.sqrt(fitted.size) / norm

        stress = float(np.sum((distances - fitted) ** 2))
        normalized_stress = _stress_1(distances, fitted)

        # Guttman transform. Zero distances would divide by zero; they also
        # contribute nothing, so their ratio is pinned to zero.
        target[upper] = fitted
        target.T[upper] = fitted
        np.fill_diagonal(target, 0.0)

        with np.errstate(divide="ignore", invalid="ignore"):
            ratio = np.where(distance_matrix > 0, target / distance_matrix, 0.0)
        guttman = -ratio
        np.fill_diagonal(guttman, 0.0)
        np.fill_diagonal(guttman, -guttman.sum(axis=1))
        points = (guttman @ points) / n

        # Convergence on the stress relative to the configuration's own size,
        # so the test does not depend on how large the numbers happen to be.
        scale = np.sum(np.sqrt(np.sum(points ** 2, axis=1)))
        normalized = stress / scale if scale > 0 else stress
        if previous is not None and abs(previous - normalized) < eps:
            break
        previous = normalized

    return points, normalized_stress, iteration


def smacof(dissimilarities, n_components: int = 2, metric: bool = True,
           n_init: int = 8, max_iter: int = 300, eps: float = 1e-6,
           random_state: int = 0):
    """
    Fit an embedding to a precomputed dissimilarity matrix.

    The first run starts from the classical MDS solution, which is
    deterministic and usually good; the rest start randomly, in case that one
    sits in a poor local minimum. The lowest-stress run wins.

    Args:
        dissimilarities: symmetric (n, n), zero diagonal
        metric: True preserves distances, False only their rank order
        n_init: how many starts to try
        random_state: pinned, so the same data always gives the same map

    Returns:
        (embedding, stress_1) where embedding is (n, n_components) and
        stress_1 is Kruskal's normalised stress — scale-invariant, so it is
        comparable between runs and between datasets.
    """
    dissimilarities = np.asarray(dissimilarities, dtype=float)
    n = dissimilarities.shape[0]
    if dissimilarities.ndim != 2 or dissimilarities.shape[1] != n:
        raise ValueError("dissimilarities must be a square matrix")
    if n <= n_components:
        # Fewer points than dimensions: the classical solution is exact.
        return classical_mds(dissimilarities, n_components), 0.0

    rng = np.random.default_rng(random_state)

    best_points, best_stress = None, np.inf
    for run in range(max(1, n_init)):
        init = classical_mds(dissimilarities, n_components) if run == 0 else None
        points, stress, _ = _smacof_single(
            dissimilarities, n_components, metric, max_iter, eps,
            init=init, rng=rng)
        # Compared on stress-1, never raw stress: see _stress_1.
        if stress < best_stress:
            best_points, best_stress = points, stress

    return best_points, float(best_stress)
